\title{The Domain Axis\\
{\large What conditions a self-feeding probe before it starts, and why it cannot be corrected for}}

% ARXIV: named. TMLR: replace with the anonymous block.

\begin{abstract}
Probes that feed a language model its own output are read as measurements of the model. We show that
such readings are dominated by a variable almost nobody reports: the tokens that condition the model
\emph{before} the loop begins. We call this the \emph{domain}. Varying it alone --- same weights,
same estimator, same geometry --- moves a discrete class label, a model ranking, and a scalar value,
by more than instruction tuning does and often by the full range of the statistic. Nine tokens of
ordinary text can take a model's fixed-point fraction from $0.21$ to $0.98$, or from $0.71$ to
$0.01$.% F154 results/text_interaction.json (Falcon3-1B-Base 0.2135 -> 0.979);
% F151 results/domain_midrange.json (gemma-2-2b-it 0.714 -> 0.005 under a 9-token prose sample) The obvious remedies all fail. The effect is not monotone in prefix length. Its direction is
not fixed: on models screened to be able to move either way, most conditioning destroys fixed-point
structure, but not all of it does. Its magnitude is not a property of the prefix: the same nine
tokens build a near-perfect funnel in two models and annihilate it in four. We report four separate
attempts to name a factor behind this --- a prose-versus-markup contrast, a universal direction, a
model-level property, a cohort difference --- each of which we withdrew within one run of proposing
it, in every case because widening the sample dissolved the factor into an interaction that had
merely been undersampled. That is the paper's central claim: on this axis there are no clean factors,
only text-by-weights pairs, so the domain cannot be corrected for and must be reported and varied.
We give the protocol that makes varying it cheap, and the anti-vacuity discipline that caught our own
withdrawals before review did.
\end{abstract}

% =================================================================================================
\section{Introduction}

A self-feeding probe reads a language model by iterating the model on its own output. The reading is
then attributed to the model: this model is more stable, that one collapses sooner, these two rank in
this order. Paper~1 \citep{veraz2026probes} showed that some such readings belong to the
\emph{construction} rather than to the model, and gave a discriminator that separates them: hold the
construction fixed and vary the model, or the reverse, and see which readings move.

This paper is about a variable that discriminator did not include, because we did not think to vary
it. Every loop starts somewhere. Before the first iterate, the model has been conditioned on
\emph{something} --- nothing at all, a BOS token, a system prompt, a chat template, a few-shot
preamble. We call that the \textbf{domain}. It is reported in almost no paper we are aware of, and it
is rarely held fixed across the comparisons those papers make.

We find that the domain dominates. It moves the readouts further than the model does, further than
instruction tuning does, and it does so in a way that resists every summary we tried to impose on it.

\paragraph{What this paper claims.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The domain moves a discrete class label, a model ranking and a scalar value, at magnitudes up
      to the full range of the statistic (\S\ref{sec:moves}).
\item It is not a length effect: the response is not monotone in the number of conditioning tokens
      (\S\ref{sec:length}).
\item Neither its direction nor its magnitude can be predicted in advance, and --- the part that
      forecloses calibration --- neither is a property of the conditioning text at all
      (\S\ref{sec:direction}).
\item Four attempts to name a factor behind the effect were each withdrawn within one run of being
      proposed, always by the same mechanism (\S\ref{sec:withdrawals}). We argue this is the
      substantive finding, not an apology for the previous three.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{What this paper does not claim.} We do not claim the effect is universal across probes; we
measure one construction. We do not offer a correction, and \S\ref{sec:direction} is our argument
that none is available. We do not claim instruct and base models differ on this axis --- we tried to
show that and failed (\S\ref{sec:withdrawals}).

% =================================================================================================
\section{Setup}

\paragraph{The estimator.} We use the \emph{short-window argmax map}: iterate
\[
  x_{t+1} \;=\; \arg\max_{x} \; p\!\left(x \mid x_{t-1}, x_{t}\right)
\]
from $\Nstarts$ random two-token starts, and census where the trajectories land. The map is
deterministic given a start, so the census has no sampling noise; its only stochasticity is the
choice of starts, controlled by a census seed. The readout we report throughout is the
\emph{fixed-point fraction} $\fpf$, the proportion of starts whose trajectory terminates in a fixed
point. Trajectories are also classified into four \emph{fixed-point classes} --- \textsc{funnel} (one
dominant attracting fixed point), \textsc{none} (no fixed points; cycles or wandering),
\textsc{fragmented} (many small basins), \textsc{borderline}.

\paragraph{The domain, operationally.} A domain is a token prefix prepended to the model's context
before every forward pass of the loop, implemented as a wrapper around the model rather than a change
to the estimator, so that the quantity being measured is provably unchanged. We report five kinds:
\textsc{raw} (no prefix), \textsc{bos} (one beginning-of-sequence token), \textsc{text} (ordinary
text, truncated to a stated token count), \textsc{template} (the model's own chat template), and
\textsc{struct} (text with high markup density, defined in \S\ref{sec:withdrawals}).

\paragraph{Resolution and tolerance.} With $\Nstarts$ starts, $\fpf$ is quantised at
$1/\Nstarts \approx 0.0104$. Throughout, a shift counts as real only if it exceeds that model's own
tolerance, defined as $\max(4/\Nstarts,\, 2\sigma)$ where $\sigma$ is the model's across-seed range
on the arm in question. Every claim below is gated at this resolution, and \S\ref{sec:discipline}
explains why we state the rule so prominently: applying a shape criterion to a quantity with no room
to vary was our most frequent error.

\paragraph{The contrast that makes this a finding rather than a truism.} It is not that any
perturbation moves these quantities. Instruction tuning is a large intervention by any behavioural
measure --- on one matched pair it moves IFEval by $+60.5$ points --- and it moves the fixed-point
class by \emph{zero}.% F143, results/argmax_census_instruct.json; IFEval from the public leaderboard
A domain change of nine tokens moves the class completely. The sensitivity is specific to the domain,
not general to perturbation.

% =================================================================================================
\section{It is not a length effect}\label{sec:length}

The natural first hypothesis is that more conditioning does more, so that the axis could be summarised
by a token count. It cannot. We swept four domains ordered by prefix length --- \textsc{raw} (0),
\textsc{bos} (1), \textsc{text} matched to that model's own template length, and \textsc{template}
--- on six instruction-tuned models.

The design's load-bearing element is the length-matched text arm: it has the same token count as the
model's chat template and none of its structure, so \textsc{text} versus \textsc{template} isolates
the \emph{kind} of prefix at fixed length, while \textsc{raw} $\to$ \textsc{bos} $\to$ \textsc{text}
traces length at roughly fixed kind. Without it, ``templates change the class'' cannot be
distinguished from ``any prefix of that length changes it''.

% F147, results/domain_gradient.json. Two of six models were excluded by the anti-vacuity gate:
% their entire span across all four domains was one census start, below their own seed noise.
Of the four models whose span was large enough to carry a shape at all, three are \textbf{not}
monotone in prefix length. One model's sequence runs $0.948 \to 0.005 \to 1.000 \to 0.000$ across
increasing prefix lengths --- a single BOS token nearly annihilating its structure, nine tokens of
ordinary prose restoring it to a \emph{perfect} funnel, and nine tokens of chat markup destroying it
again. Prefix length does not order the fixed-point structure, and a length-based correction would be
wrong.

% =================================================================================================
\section{Neither direction nor magnitude is predictable}\label{sec:direction}

\subsection{Direction}

Since length fails, the next hope is sign: perhaps conditioning always destroys structure, so at
least the direction of the bias is known. Testing this requires models with room to move
\emph{both} ways --- a model at $\fpf = 0.000$ can only go up, one at $0.98$ can only go down, and
scoring such models tells you about the floor rather than about the domain.

% F149, results/domain_direction.json -- scoring only where the baseline could have been wrong left
% 1 of 6 models and 2 units.
Our first attempt failed on exactly this. Scoring a floor/ceiling baseline only where it \emph{could
have been wrong} left one model and two units out of six models; the unrestricted version of the same
baseline reports ``9 of 9 correct, 100\%, direction is mechanical'', where every one of those nine
units came from a model that could not have contradicted it.

% F150, results/midrange_screen.json
We therefore screened for the missing instrument --- one cheap census per candidate, keeping models
whose $\fpf$ lands in $[0.2, 0.8]$ with headroom exceeding their own tolerance on both sides. The
screen is instructive in itself: of seven instruct candidates, four sat at $0.000$ and one at
$0.990$. Extreme values are typical, which is why this question is usually unanswerable by accident.

% F152, results/domain_base.json -- 35 arms on 7 readable base models: 32 down, 2 up, 1 flat.
On nine screened models across two cohorts, most conditioning does reduce fixed-point structure ---
but not all of it. Two base models move \emph{both} ways from a single raw value:
\texttt{Falcon3-1B-Base} rises from $0.214$ to $0.906$ under one BOS token and falls to $0.000$ under
nine tokens of prose; \texttt{Minerva-3B-base} falls to $0.000$ under one nine-token prose sample and
rises to $0.786$ under another \emph{of the same length}. Weights fixed, starting value fixed, only
the domain varying: no floor or ceiling can produce that.

\subsection{Magnitude, and why it is not a property of the prefix}

% F154, results/text_interaction.json -- p1 is Pile row 101, a table of contents.
The strongest form of the result is Table~\ref{tab:p1}. A single nine-token prefix --- Pile row 101,
the opening of a table of contents, \verb|"\n\nGreat Britain\n\n# Contents\n"| --- was applied
unchanged to six models screened for headroom.

\begin{table}[t]\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrl}
\toprule
model & raw $\fpf$ & under the prefix & \\
\midrule
Falcon3-1B-Base       & 0.214 & \textbf{0.979} & up \\
Minerva-3B-base       & 0.328 & \textbf{1.000} & up \\
pythia-410m-deduped   & 0.427 & 0.016 & down \\
Qwen1.5-1.8B          & 0.510 & 0.000 & down \\
SmolLM-1.7B           & 0.562 & 0.000 & down \\
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct & 0.573 & 0.005 & down \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The same nine tokens, six models. It builds a near-perfect funnel in two and annihilates it
in four. Source: F154, \texttt{results/text\_interaction.json}.}
\label{tab:p1}
\end{table}

This is what forecloses correction. A reader who accepts that the domain matters will reach for the
obvious fix: characterise prefixes, publish a list of safe ones. Table~\ref{tab:p1} says that cannot
work --- not because prefix effects are unshared, but because they are \emph{opposite}. The single
most structure-building prefix we measured is also among the most destructive, depending on which
weights receive it. A predictor study on text features would have to predict the interaction, not the
text.

\section{Four withdrawals, and why they are the result}\label{sec:withdrawals}

We proposed four factors that would have made the domain tractable. We withdrew all four, each within
one run of proposing it, and in every case for the same reason: widening the sample dissolved the
factor into an interaction that had merely been undersampled.

\begin{table}[t]\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
claim & died on & source \\
\midrule
``prose and markup differ, and the sign flips by model'' & mid-range models & F147 $\to$ F151 \\
``the effect is unidirectional: 18 of 18 arms down''      & a wider model set & F151 $\to$ F152 \\
``no text raises two models''                             & a wider corpus & F153 $\to$ F154 \\
``bidirectionality is a model property''                  & a wider text class & F154 $\to$ F155 \\
``instruct models resist raising''                        & ONE additional text & F156 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Every factor we named was withdrawn within one run. The mechanism was the same each time.}
\label{tab:withdrawals}
\end{table}

Two are worth stating in full because of what they cost.

% F151, results/domain_midrange.json -> F152, results/domain_base.json
\paragraph{A universal from $n=2$.} On two mid-range instruct models, all $18$ domain arms moved
down, and every apparent up-shift in the programme to that point turned out to be mechanical --- one
saturating exactly at the ceiling, one inside its own seed spread, one starting from the floor. We
wrote ``the domain effect is unidirectional, without exception''. Seven base models produced two
bidirectional counterexamples immediately.

% F155, results/structural_text.json -> F156, results/instruct_raisable.json
\paragraph{A null we wanted.} After finding that structural text (markup density $\geq 0.15$ over the
first 200 characters, the Pile's 95th percentile) raises some models more often than prose does, we
noted that two instruct models resisted every text tried. We pre-registered that a null here would be
\emph{the first factor in this programme to survive a widening} --- a positive structural claim the
paper otherwise lacks --- and said so before running. One text of twelve refused it: a C source-file
header takes \texttt{gemma-2-2b-it} from $0.714$ to $0.917$. We report the null we wanted and did not
get.

\paragraph{What survives.} A rate difference: instruct models were raised on $1$ of $24$ text-model
units against $11$ of $48$ for base models on the \emph{same} twelve texts. With two instruct clusters
this cannot be tested, and Table~\ref{tab:withdrawals} is four consecutive instances of exactly this
kind of gap dissolving. We record it as a lead and decline to promote it.

\paragraph{The claim.} On this axis there are no clean factors --- only text-by-weights pairs. We
state this not as a summary of failures but as the most robust structural finding here: it is the one
claim that survived every widening we applied, precisely because each widening was an attempt to
replace it with something stronger.

% =================================================================================================
\section{The discipline that caught this}\label{sec:discipline}

The withdrawals above were found by design, not in review, and the mechanism is worth reporting
because it generalises past this instrument.

\paragraph{A criterion with a shape must not be applied to a quantity with no room to vary.} Our most
frequent error, by a wide margin. Instances: flat sequences scored as monotone-or-not when their
entire span was one census start; a single trajectory in $\Nstarts$ flipping a monotonicity verdict;
two floored arms counted as ``agreement'' when neither could disagree; a baseline scoring
$9/9 = 100\%$ where no unit could have contradicted it; and, twice, the defect appearing inside the
anti-vacuity gate written to prevent it --- once excluding the most decisive model in a run while
admitting one whose whole effect was half a census start.

\paragraph{Its sibling: a criterion applied where it cannot \emph{yet} fail.} A confident universal
from $n=2$ is not vacuous in the same way --- a counterexample was possible --- but it was unlikely
enough that the claim was never really at risk. Both are cheap to catch by widening before claiming.

\paragraph{The protocol.} (i) Screen for headroom before testing direction; (ii) gate each question
separately, because ``is the contrast robust'' needs the gap to be real while ``is the value stable''
needs the values off the floor; (iii) judge each shift against its own noise, not a pooled tolerance;
(iv) verify anti-vacuity rather than assume it, even when the models were selected for it; (v) refuse
tests that cannot fail informatively at the available $n$, and say so before seeing the numbers.
Point (v) is not rhetorical: we declined to compute predictors of shift magnitude on six clusters,
and declined a significance test on three, in both cases recording the refusal in the
pre-registration.

\paragraph{Pooling.} One consistency gate deserves separate mention. Structural text raised two of
three models more often than prose, and the pooled ratio ($7/18$ vs $3/18$) cleared our
pre-registered bar --- but the third model reversed. A gate added before the verdict refused to read
the pooled number, on the grounds that pooling across units pointing different ways is a Simpson's
shape. Without it we would have reported ``the first predictive statement'' in this programme.

% =================================================================================================
\section{Limits}

\paragraph{One construction.} We measure the short-window argmax map. That the domain dominates
\emph{this} probe does not establish it dominates self-consistency, iterated refinement, or agentic
loops, though all condition a model before iterating and none, to our knowledge, reports the domain.

\paragraph{Small cohorts.} The largest single comparison here is six models and twelve texts.
Table~\ref{tab:withdrawals} is the reason we state boundaries in the specific form ``these models
resisted these texts'' rather than in the general form: four times, the general form was wrong.

\paragraph{One length, one corpus, three sources.} The interaction results fix the prefix at nine
tokens and draw text from The Pile, Shakespeare, and one written paragraph. ``Structural'' has one
operationalisation. A different length or corpus could change the rates, though not the existence
results.

\paragraph{Confounds we could not break.} \texttt{gemma-2-2b-it} is the only \textsc{fragmented}
model in our domain cohort, so class and cohort are confounded in it. \texttt{Falcon3-3B-Instruct} is
excluded from direction work entirely: its raw census varies $0.615$--$0.792$ across four seeds, so
its tolerance swamps every domain shift it has.% F150, results/midrange_screen.json

\paragraph{PENDING --- prior art.} The novelty gate for the domain claim specifically has not been
run. Paper~1's gate covered the fixed-point-class claim; the literature on prompt sensitivity and
prefix conditioning is large and adjacent, and this section must not be written before that gate.

% =================================================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

The tokens that condition a language model before a self-feeding loop begins dominate what the loop
reports. The effect is large, is not ordered by prefix length, and has neither a predictable direction
nor a predictable magnitude. It is not a property of the conditioning text: the same nine tokens
build a near-perfect funnel in some models and annihilate it in others. We tried four times to find a
factor underneath it and withdrew each attempt within a run, always because widening the sample
turned the factor into an interaction. The practical consequence is narrow and firm: the domain
cannot be corrected for, so it must be reported and varied. The package that makes varying it cheap
ships with this paper.
